title: Assuming TCP Guarantees span Multiple Connection Sessions
pattern: Re-establishing a broken TCP socket or streaming connection and resending unacknowledged data directly, under the assumption that the underlying network protocol's packet-level duplicate-detection and ordering guarantees span across distinct connection sessions.
why_bad: TCP only guarantees ordered, duplicate-free packet delivery within the scope of a single, active socket session [37]. Once a connection is closed or reset, any subsequent socket connection is an entirely blank slate [37]. Resending unacknowledged data on a new session can easily lead to duplicate execution because the server may have processed the original packet but failed to return the TCP ACK before the socket broke [21, 31, 32].
detection: Identify methods that catch errors on socket writes, instantiate a new socket/stream connection, and immediately retry the exact same raw payload write without appending application-level session recovery tokens, sequence IDs, or idempotency keys.
fix: Do not treat TCP as an application-level exactly-once link across reconnections. Always embed application-level sequence numbers, epoch tokens, or transaction IDs inside resent payloads to let the recipient deduplicate writes [32, 33, 34].
source: Alex Petrov, *Database Internals*, Chapter 8 (Perfect Links) / passages [36, 37]; Martin Kleppmann, *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, Chapter 8 (Unreliable Networks) / passages [21, 31, 32].
